source_refs.note: Topic 2.6.1.5 List Operations (PDF 52-53, printed 49-50). The book names a variable 'slice', which hides Python's built-in slice; the lesson uses 'part'. MCQ 10 is answered.

blocks.text: Lists also support operations such as slicing (taking part of a list) and concatenation (joining lists with +).

blocks.title: Python code (each .... is one 4-space indent)
blocks.text:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
part = numbers[1:4]    # items at index 1 to 3
combined = part + [6, 7]
print(combined)    # [2, 3, 4, 6, 7]

blocks.prompt: Class activity: books = ["To Kill a Mockingbird", "1984", "The Great Gatsby", "Pride and Prejudice"]. Add "Moby Dick", replace "1984" with "Brave New World", remove "The Great Gatsby", merge with ["War and Peace", "Hamlet"] and print. What is the result?
blocks.explanation: books.append("Moby Dick"); books[1] = "Brave New World"; books.remove("The Great Gatsby"); books = books + ["War and Peace", "Hamlet"]; the list is To Kill a Mockingbird, Brave New World, Pride and Prejudice, Moby Dick, War and Peace, Hamlet.

items: Slicing list[a:b] (b excluded); + joins lists; sort and remove can be combined.
